description_full: Arm Holdings plc researches, develops, licenses, and markets central processing unit (CPU) intellectual property (IP), graphics processing unit IP, systems IP, compute subsystems (CSS), and associated software, tools and related services. The company provides a product portfolio, including CPU IP, GPU and neural processing unit (NPU) accelerators, system IP such as interconnects, compute platform products including pre-integrated CSSs, and development tools and software. The company serves semiconductor companies, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), cloud service providers (CSPs), and organizations developing chips for end markets such as smartphones, consumer electronics, industrial IoT, embedded systems, cloud data centers, networking, automotive, and robotics. It provides its products and services in the United States, China, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, and internationally. The company was founded in 1990 and is based in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Arm Holdings plc operates as a subsidiary of SoftBank Group Corp.
ceo_bio: Mr. Rene Anthony Andrada  Haas | CEO & Director | Age 63 | Compensation: $5.1M (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 9K people. Revenue per employee of $513K ranks in the above the sector median among Technology peers, with revenue growing 23%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $102K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $110K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 10× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Arm Holdings plc is a mega-cap technology business with a $203.9B market cap on $4.9B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +23% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +7.4pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at 16% against a 11% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 97% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $979M in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.69× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and stock-based comp at 21% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 11pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 82% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 28% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 58% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 83% and a beta of 1.41, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.1B traded a day.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $16.73 (margin of safety -1039%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 14%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $10.82 to $27.11 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 219.0 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 186.8 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 208.2 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 40 covering analysts target $272 on average, 43% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 11.4%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.68).
It runs a 97% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow, or -1% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.69x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 56.4% of revenue on R&D and 21.4% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $3.6B (2% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 52.5, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 23.4% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 16.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.97, a backlog worth 42% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 15%.
Capex runs 2.2x depreciation (11.1% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.4% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (14 sales, net $38.4M sold).
Short interest is elevated at 10.7% of the float, 3.3 days to cover.
people: With about 9,584 employees, each generates about $513K of revenue, 1.4x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 23.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $102K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.1M (10x revenue per employee).
